hypothesis: A statically stable four-wheeled centaur base (wide 0.40 m track, short legs, low CoM) will survive the lateral shove like the wheeled seed while achieving clearly positive flat and rough speed, because it removes the dynamic balancing problem that left the biped wheel seed stationary and made the walking seeds fall or drift.
inspiration: Automotive skid-steer platforms and the ANYmal-on-wheels / Swiss-Mile wheel-legged quadruped

hypothesis: Widening the four-wheeled centaur's track to 0.45 m, lengthening its wheelbase to 0.7 m, shortening its legs and chest to lower the CoM, and stiffening its knee springs into suspension will stop the tip-overs on flat ground and under the shove. Raising torque to 120 Nm should also let the wheels climb rubble. Together these should keep flat speed near 1.5 m/s and raise rough speed well above parent 4's 0.034 m/s.
inspiration: automotive rover suspension (wide-track, long-wheelbase, low-CoM vehicles like Mars rovers and rock crawlers)

hypothesis: Lengthening child 5's legs from 0.17 to 0.23 m should raise ground clearance and suspension travel. Stiffening the knee springs to 130 Nm/rad and raising torque to 170 Nm should let the wheels climb rubble instead of stalling. Together these should lift rough speed well above 0.07 m/s while flat speed stays above 1.4 m/s. A lower 0.25 m chest and the maximal 0.45 m track should offset the higher CoM, so the robot still survives the shove.
inspiration: rocker-style planetary rovers and trophy-truck long-travel suspension; ANYmal-on-wheels leg-wheel hybrids

hypothesis: Changing only child 5's foot_len from 0.18 to 0.30 m should raise rough-terrain speed well above 0.07 m/s while keeping flat speed above 1.4 m/s and still surviving the shove; this assumes the wheel radius scales with foot length, so the larger wheel meets rubble at a shallower angle and rolls over it instead of stalling (a test of whether wheel size, not torque or leg length, limits rough speed).
inspiration: automotive off-road design: larger tire diameter raises step-climbing ability (obstacle height ≈ wheel radius) more effectively than added torque

hypothesis: Enabling an actuated spine pitch joint (with a 80 Nm/rad passive spring) on child 7 should raise rough-terrain speed well above 0.176 m/s while keeping flat speed above 1.4 m/s and surviving the shove. The articulated chassis lets the front and rear wheel pairs pitch independently, like a rocker-bogie or articulated loader, so all four wheels stay loaded and keep traction over rubble instead of one axle hanging and stalling.
inspiration: Mars rover rocker-bogie suspension and articulated-frame construction loaders; cheetah spine flexion

hypothesis: Changing only run 7's knee_spring from 90 to 50 Nm/rad should raise rough-terrain speed above 0.176 m/s while flat speed stays near 1.6 m/s and the robot still survives the shove. Softer suspension should let each wheel comply over rubble and keep all four wheels loaded for traction, where a stiff knee lifts a wheel or bounces the chassis. Any sag from the softer spring only lowers the CoM, which should help push survival. This is the remaining wheel-side lever, because foot_len is already at its 0.30 m schema maximum and leg_pairs cannot exceed 2.
inspiration: Off-road trophy-truck and rally suspension: low spring rates with long compliant travel keep the tyres in ground contact on rough terrain; also the compliant leg tendons of goats on scree

hypothesis: Changing only run 9's knee_spring from 50 to 20 Nm/rad should raise rough-terrain speed above 0.356 m/s, while flat speed stays near 1.6 m/s and the shove is still survived. Softening from 90 to 50 already doubled rough speed (0.176 to 0.356), so suspension compliance looks like the active lever. Even softer knees should keep all four big wheels loaded on rubble, and any sag only lowers the CoM. If rough speed falls or the chassis bottoms out, the compliance optimum lies between 20 and 50.
inspiration: Long-travel soft suspension on desert trophy trucks and the compliant passive suspension of planetary rovers

hypothesis: Changing only run 9's knee_dir from backward to forward should raise rough-terrain speed above 0.356 m/s while flat speed stays near 1.6 m/s and the shove is still survived. With the knee pointing forward, a rubble impact that pushes the wheel back and up acts along the leg's compliant direction, like a trailing-arm suspension. The 50 Nm/rad knee spring can then absorb the bump instead of jamming the wheel against the obstacle. If rough speed falls, the backward (leading-link) geometry is the better choice for climbing.
inspiration: automotive trailing-arm vs leading-link suspension geometry; motorcycle and aircraft landing-gear trailing links

hypothesis: Changing only run 9's knee_spring from 50 to 40 Nm/rad should raise rough-terrain speed above 0.356 m/s while flat speed stays near 1.6 m/s and the shove is still survived. Rough speed peaked at 50 and collapsed at 20, which suggests an optimum somewhere in 30–50. A modest softening should add wheel compliance on rubble without the roll softness that cost push survival at 20. If rough speed falls or the shove fails, the optimum lies at or above 50.
inspiration: automotive suspension tuning: bracketing spring rate between ride compliance and roll stiffness

hypothesis: Changing only run 9's knee_spring from 50 to 60 Nm/rad should keep rough-terrain speed at or above 0.356 m/s, keep flat speed near 1.6 m/s, and survive the shove with more margin. Softer springs (40, 20) collapsed rough speed and failed the push, and 90 gave only 0.176, so the compliance optimum is narrow and likely sits between 50 and 70. Slightly stiffer roll support should make push survival more robust without losing much wheel compliance on rubble. If rough speed drops below 0.3, the peak is sharply at 50.
inspiration: automotive suspension tuning: balancing spring rate for ride compliance against roll stiffness

hypothesis: Changing only run 13's knee_spring from 60 to 70 Nm/rad should raise rough-terrain speed above 0.555 m/s, keep flat speed near 1.62 m/s, and still survive the shove. Rough speed rose steeply from 50 (0.356) to 60 (0.555) and is known to drop by 90 (0.176), so the compliance peak may lie between 60 and 80. If rough speed falls below 0.555, the peak sits at or just below 60, and the next probe should be 65.
inspiration: automotive suspension tuning: sweeping spring rate to balance tyre contact (grip) against roll stiffness

hypothesis: Changing only run 13's ankle_spring from 0 to 30 Nm/rad should raise rough-terrain speed above 0.555 m/s, keep flat speed near 1.62 m/s and still survive the shove. A passive ankle spring acts as a second, series compliance stage at the wheel mount, like a tyre sidewall or a bushing on top of the main spring, so the big wheels can follow rubble without softening the 60 Nm/rad knee spring that supplies roll support. The 70 Nm/rad collapse (0.047) shows the knee-spring axis is too sharp or noisy to tune further. If rough speed falls below 0.35 or the shove fails, ankle compliance destabilises the wheel contact and should stay at 0.
inspiration: Automotive two-stage suspension (coil spring plus compliant tyre and bushing), and the series tendon-plus-muscle compliance at the distal ankle in ungulates

hypothesis: Changing only run 13's knee_spring from 60 to 55 Nm/rad, between two successful runs (50: 0.356 and 60: 0.555), should give rough speed of at least 0.35 m/s, flat speed near 1.62 m/s and a survived shove; a collapse below 0.1 would show that rough speed is dominated by ES or terrain noise rather than a real compliance optimum, and that the 60 result was a lucky outlier.
inspiration: automotive suspension tuning: bracketing the spring rate between two known-good settings to separate a real optimum from test-to-test variance

hypothesis: Changing only run 13's max_torque from 120 to 150 Nm should raise rough-terrain speed above 0.2 m/s, consistently rather than by luck, while flat speed stays near 1.62 m/s and the shove is still survived. The erratic spring results (50: 0.356, 55: 0.112, 60: 0.555, 70: 0.047) suggest the wheels sit at the edge of stalling on rubble edges, so extra wheel and hip torque headroom should push the climb past that threshold and make it robust to gait-tuning noise. If rough speed stays below 0.15, torque is not the limiter and the variance comes from ES or terrain noise.
inspiration: automotive low-range gearing and the torque reserve of crawler/rock-crawler drivetrains

hypothesis: Adding only a short 0.25 m actuated tail to run 13 should raise rough-terrain speed above 0.2 m/s more consistently than the noisy spring and torque probes (0.047–0.555), keep flat speed near 1.62 m/s and still survive the shove. Like a cheetah's or a wheelie bar's counterweight, the tail lets the gait shift pitch load onto the front wheels at rubble edges so they climb instead of stalling. If rough speed stays below 0.15 or the shove fails, pitch balance is not the limiter.
inspiration: cheetah and kangaroo tail pitch stabilisation; anti-wheelie bars on drag cars and the rear stabiliser on stair-climbing tracked robots

hypothesis: A near-exact replicate of run 13, changing only knee_spring from 60 to 61 Nm/rad, should give rough speed of at least 0.3 m/s, flat speed near 1.62 m/s and a survived shove if run 13's 0.555 m/s is a reproducible property of this chassis. A result below 0.2 m/s would mark run 13 as a lucky ES or terrain draw and set the honest baseline for this chassis at roughly 0.05–0.18 m/s, against which bold geometric changes must be judged.
inspiration: none (experimental-design replicate, like a repeat trial in materials testing to estimate scatter before claiming an effect)

hypothesis: A 'high-clearance, long-wheelbase' package on run 13's chassis should give rough speed above 0.3 m/s in this run and in a replicate, clearly above the replicated 0.05–0.18 m/s baseline (run 19: 0.071), while flat speed stays near 1.62 m/s and the shove is still survived. The package lengthens the wheelbase to 0.8 m so the chassis bridges rubble gaps, and lengthens the shins to 0.22 m so the belly and knees stop high-centering on rubble. To keep the CoM low for push safety, it compensates with a lower chest (0.25 m) and shorter arms (0.3 m). Rough speed below 0.2 means clearance and wheelbase are not the limiter. A failed shove means the taller legs cost too much roll stability.
inspiration: rock-crawler and off-road vehicle design (ground clearance plus long wheelbase for breakover angle), with the low-slung mass placement of military 4x4s

hypothesis: Run 20's package without its longer shins (shins back to 0.17 m, keeping the 0.8 m wheelbase, 0.25 m chest and 0.3 m arms) on run 13's chassis should survive the shove again. If it does, the 0.22 m shins caused run 20's push failure. The longer wheelbase and lower, lighter upper body should then give rough speed above 0.3 m/s, against the replicated 0.05–0.18 m/s baseline (run 19: 0.071). Rough speed below 0.2 would mean wheelbase and CoM height are not rough-terrain levers.
inspiration: long-wheelbase off-road trucks and rock crawlers: a longer wheelbase bridges rubble, and a low centre of mass keeps the vehicle from tipping

hypothesis: A near-exact replicate of run 21 (0.8 m wheelbase, 0.25 m chest, 0.3 m arms, 0.17 m legs), changing only knee_spring from 60 to 61 Nm/rad, should again give rough speed above 0.3 m/s, with flat speed near 1.62 m/s and a survived shove. That would confirm that the longer wheelbase and lower, lighter upper body are a real rough-terrain lever. A result below 0.2 m/s would mark run 21's 0.576 m/s as a lucky draw like run 13, since run 13's own replicate (run 19) fell to 0.071.
inspiration: automotive long-wheelbase off-road chassis (bridging and low CoM), plus experimental-design replication practice

hypothesis: Lowering only run 22's chest_height from 0.25 to 0.20 m (spring back to 60) continues the lever confirmed by runs 21 and 22 (rough 0.576 and 1.332, against the 0.07 baseline). A lower, lighter upper body should keep the front wheels loaded and resist pitch-over at rubble edges, so rough speed should stay above 0.5 m/s with flat speed near 1.62 m/s and the shove survived. Rough speed below 0.3 would mean the upper-body gain is already saturated at 0.25 m, or that wheelbase rather than CoM height drove it.
inspiration: Low-slung rally cars and the low CoM of rocker-bogie rovers. Lowering the sprung mass cuts weight transfer and pitch-over on obstacles.
